textTitles: Hartley Town Library — joining and borrowing
Green Lane car boot sale — stallholders

texts.label: A
texts.title: Hartley Town Library — joining and borrowing

paragraphs.text: Hartley Town Library — joining and borrowing. Membership is free to anyone who lives, works or studies in the district, and you may join online or at the desk; if you join online, bring proof of address to your first visit or the card will not be activated. Children under twelve are registered by an adult, who accepts responsibility for items taken out on that card. A replacement card costs £2, and the first replacement for a child is free.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Members may hold twelve items at a time, of which no more than four may be films. Books are lent for three weeks and renewed twice, unless another member has reserved them; films are lent for one week and are not renewed. Reservations cost 50p and you are told by text or email when the item arrives, after which it is held at the desk for six days. Overdue books are charged at 20p a day up to a maximum of £8 per item, and children’s items carry no charge.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The building is open from 9 am to 7 pm on weekdays, to 4 pm on Saturdays and not at all on Sundays. The computers may be used free for one hour a day by members, and printing costs 10p a page in black and 40p in colour. The meeting room upstairs is lent to community groups without charge on weekday evenings; it must be booked at least a week ahead and is not available to commercial organisations. Please do not eat in the reading room; drinks with lids are allowed.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Green Lane car boot sale — stallholders

paragraphs.text: Green Lane car boot sale — information for stallholders. The sale runs every Sunday from April to October in the field behind the leisure centre. Sellers arrive from 6 am and the public is admitted at 8 am; nothing may be sold before the public gate opens. A pitch costs £12 for a car, £18 for a van and £25 for a van with a trailer, paid in cash at the gate. No booking is taken and pitches are allocated in the order vehicles arrive.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: You may sell second-hand household goods, clothing, books, toys and plants. You may not sell food or drink of any kind, animals, fuel, medicines, knives or anything new and unused in commercial quantities; the organiser may ask a seller to pack up, without a refund, if this rule is broken. Traders bringing new goods should apply for the separate trade area, which costs £40 and requires a copy of your public liability insurance.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Sellers must take home whatever they have not sold. The bins at the gate are for the public and not for stock, and a seller who leaves goods beside a bin will not be admitted again. Toilets are in the leisure centre and open from 7 am. The field closes at 2 pm and vehicles must be off the grass by 2.30, as the sports pitches are used in the afternoon. In wet weather the sale is cancelled by 6 am and a notice is put on the gate and on the village page.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Food hygiene: what every member of café staff must know. Before your first shift you complete the basic food hygiene course online, which takes about two hours, and the certificate is kept in your file; the course is repeated every three years. Hands are washed on arrival, after handling raw food, after touching your face or hair, after taking out rubbish and after using the toilet. The sink by the door is for hands only, never for rinsing equipment, and the blue paper beside it is for drying hands.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Temperatures decide most of what we do. The fridges run between one and five degrees and are checked twice a day, at opening and at four o’clock, and the reading is written on the sheet on the fridge door. Hot food is held above sixty-three degrees and anything that has been out of temperature for more than two hours is thrown away, not cooled and kept. Frozen deliveries are put away within fifteen minutes of arriving, and nothing is ever refrozen once it has thawed.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Raw and ready-to-eat foods are kept apart at every stage. Raw meat sits on the bottom shelf of the fridge so that nothing can drip onto anything else; boards and knives are colour-coded and are not carried between areas; the cloth used on a surface where raw food has been prepared goes straight into the wash. If you are unsure whether a surface is clean, clean it again, and never wipe a board and put it back on the rack.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Allergens are the part of the job where guessing is dangerous. Fourteen allergens must be declared, the information is in the folder at the counter, and it must be given to any customer who asks, by reading from the folder rather than from memory. If a customer says they have an allergy, tell the kitchen before the order goes on; if a dish cannot be made safely, say so rather than hoping. Staff who feel unwell with stomach illness must not work with food and must stay away for forty-eight hours after the symptoms stop.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Training and study leave: what the company offers. Every employee has a training budget of £600 a year, which does not carry over into the following year. It may be spent on courses, conferences, books or software that relate to your current role or to a role you could reasonably move into, and it is agreed with your manager rather than claimed afterwards. The company also pays for any training it requires you to do, and that spending does not come out of your £600.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Study leave applies to qualifications that take longer than a term. For a part-time qualification related to your work, the company pays the course fee and gives one day a fortnight of paid leave for the length of the course, plus five days of paid leave for revision and examinations. The agreement is written down before the course begins and includes a repayment clause: if you leave within a year of finishing, half the fee is repaid; within two years, a quarter; after two years, nothing.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Applications are made twice a year, in March and September, and are decided by the department head with the training manager. Where more applications arrive than the budget allows, priority goes first to qualifications the team needs and cannot buy in, second to people who have not had study leave before. A refusal is explained in writing, and an application that was refused because of budget rather than merit is carried automatically into the next round without being rewritten.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Two conditions apply to everything above. You must remain in the job while studying, so study leave cannot be taken as a block at the end of a course, and the days cannot be saved up. And you are asked to share what you learned: a short session for your team, a written summary in the company wiki, or a lunchtime talk. This is not a formality; the training manager reports each year on what was learned and shared, and the budget for the following year is argued for on the strength of it.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The rural bus is the part of public transport that nobody photographs. It carries school children, people going to hospital appointments, workers on shifts that do not fit a car-sharing arrangement and older people who no longer drive, and it does so in vehicles that are usually half empty for most of the day. That emptiness is the whole of the problem: a service that runs when it is needed is a service that runs when it is not, and the cost is counted per journey while the value is felt per person.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Decline followed a familiar sequence in most countries. Car ownership rose, passenger numbers fell, operators cut the routes that lost the most money, and the cuts fell first on evenings and Sundays. A service that does not run in the evening cannot be used to get to an evening job, so the people who might have used it bought a car or moved, and the next round of figures justified the next round of cuts. Nothing in that sequence required a bad decision by anybody.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The money behind a rural route is rarely what passengers imagine. Fares typically cover a third to a half of the cost on a country route, with the rest coming from local authority contracts, from concessionary travel payments for older passengers, and from cross-subsidy by the operator’s profitable urban routes. When the urban routes stopped being profitable, that last source disappeared quietly, and several networks that looked stable collapsed within two years for reasons that had nothing to do with the villages they served.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Demand-responsive services were offered as the answer and have had mixed results. Instead of a timetable, passengers book a journey by telephone or app and a small vehicle collects them; in principle the bus goes where people are rather than where the timetable says. In practice the schemes that work serve a defined area with a simple booking rule and a vehicle that is already paid for; the ones that fail are those sold as a technology, where the software cost more than the driver and the elderly passengers who most needed the service found the booking harder than the timetable.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: School transport is the hidden foundation of the system. In many districts the only reason a vehicle and a driver exist at all is the statutory duty to carry children to school, and the public route that runs at ten in the morning exists because the same bus and driver would otherwise be idle between the runs. Where school contracts have been separated from public routes for procurement reasons, the public service has often disappeared, which is an example of a rule that saved money in one budget and cost more in another.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Communities have filled gaps themselves, within limits. Volunteer car schemes, community minibuses and dial-a-ride services run in thousands of places and are genuinely valuable, but they depend on a small number of people, they cover journeys that can be planned rather than journeys that cannot, and their coordinators are typically in their seventies. A model that relies on volunteers is a model with a succession problem, and the district that loses two organisers in a year loses the service with them.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What the evidence supports is unglamorous and consistent. A route that runs at a regular interval is used more than one with the same number of buses at irregular times, because a passenger does not need a timetable to use it; a route that connects to a train or a market on the right day carries more people than one that arrives ten minutes after the connection leaves; and a fare structure that is simple is worth more than a discount that is complicated. None of this requires new technology, and all of it requires somebody to be responsible for the whole network rather than for each route.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The honest framing is that a rural bus is not a business and does not become one. It is a public service with a cost, like a rural road or a village school, and the choice is whether to pay for it rather than whether to make it pay. Countries that treat it that way run services that are thin but reliable; countries that wait for a commercial answer end up with nothing in the evening, a volunteer car in the morning and a growing number of people who cannot get to the places where the services they need have been concentrated.
paragraphs.label: H
